## Defects found

**1. Mutable default argument (`seen=[]`)**
The default list is created once, at function-definition time, and shared across every call that doesn't pass its own `seen`. Because the function also `.append()`s into it, state leaks between unrelated calls: scores seen on call 1 will silently suppress those same values from appearing in `result` on call 2, call 3, etc., even though each call presumably wants an independent "top N" computation. This also means the function is not safely reentrant/thread-safe and results depend on call history, not just on the current `scores` argument.

**2. `range(0, limit)` indexes past the end of `scores` → `IndexError`**
The loop always iterates `limit` times and blindly does `scores[i]`, but never checks that `scores` actually has `limit` elements. If `len(scores) < limit` (e.g. the default `limit=5` with a 3-element list, or any empty list), this raises `IndexError: list index out of range` instead of just returning however many scores are available.

**3. Duplicate scores cause fewer than `limit` results even when enough distinct values exist**
The loop only ever looks at the first `limit` positions of the sorted list (`i` in `range(0, limit)`); when a value at one of those positions is already in `seen` (e.g., because it duplicates an earlier position in the *same* top-`limit` window), it is skipped rather than being replaced by the next distinct candidate further down the list. E.g. `scores = [10,10,10,10,10,3,2,1]` with `limit=5` sorts to the same list, and every index 0–4 is `10`; only the first `10` gets added (the rest are already "seen"), so `result == [10]` instead of the 4 distinct top values `[10, 3, 2, 1]` that were available in the list. This defeats the apparent intent of returning up to `limit` (distinct) top scores — it returns however many distinct values happen to occupy the first `limit` sorted slots, which can be far fewer.

**4. `scores.sort(reverse=True)` mutates the caller's original list as a side effect**
Sorting in place reorders the list object the caller passed in, rather than working on a copy. Any code in the caller that holds a reference to that same list and relies on its original order will see it silently reordered after calling `top_scores`, which is a surprising side effect for a function that looks like it just computes and returns values.

These are the defects present; I did not find issues with the descending sort direction or with computing the average over all scores, since both are stated as intended.
